entries.name: Epic / High Fantasy
entries.description: The full secondary world: deep history, civilizational stakes, and a canvas larger than any one life.
entries.principle: Scale is the contract — an invented world with its own geography, ages, peoples, and metaphysics, threatened at civilizational level, resolved by characters whose choices ripple across the map. Length is a feature rather than an indulgence; the reader is buying immersion and consequence at historical scale, and the ending must feel like history turning rather than a problem solved.
entries.example: Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings set every term (deep time, invented languages, appendices as proof of the iceberg); Jordan's Wheel of Time and Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire industrialized the multi-POV epic; Sanderson's Stormlight Archive is the contemporary engineering standard; Jemisin's Broken Earth won three consecutive Hugos by making the world's structure the story's argument.
entries.application: Build the iceberg before the plot — histories, languages, and grudges the story only glances at — then show the reader a tenth of it. Multi-POV is the form's default engine, so give each thread its own arc rather than treating viewpoints as camera positions. The known failure point is the middle: epics sag when map-crossing outpaces character change, so schedule a reversal that resets the political board at the halfway mark.

entries.name: Sword & Sorcery
entries.description: Mercenary heroes, immediate stakes, and magic as menace rather than utility.
entries.principle: The counter-epic: no chosen one, no world to save — a rogue, thief, or barbarian working for pay, survival, or grudge, in episodic adventures where sorcery is corrupt, alien, and usually the antagonist's instrument. Pace is the promise; the reader wants forward motion, sensory atmosphere, and a protagonist who leaves town at the end with nothing permanently settled.
entries.example: Howard's Conan founded it in the pulps; Leiber's Fafhrd and the Gray Mouser gave it wit, friendship, and its name; Moorcock's Elric inverted the hero into a doomed, drug-dependent aristocrat; Wagner's Kane darkened it further. The modern revival runs through Abercrombie's shorter work and the grimdark strain.
entries.application: Keep stakes personal and portable — a theft, a debt, a rescue — and let the world stay unmapped beyond the story's edge. Magic should cost or corrupt whoever wields it; if your sorcery is a convenient toolkit, you have drifted into epic. Short forms suit the tradition, which was built on novelettes: treat the episodic structure as an asset to exploit rather than a limitation to escape.

entries.name: Grimdark
entries.description: Epic fantasy with the consolation removed: moral ambiguity, real consequence, and no promised restoration.
entries.principle: A deliberate reaction against the genre's comfort contract — protagonists are compromised, victories cost more than they return, institutions are corrupt structurally rather than through villainy, and the world declines to reorganize itself around virtue. The register is not merely violent but disenchanted: the reader is promised that the story will not lie to them about how power works.
entries.example: Cook's The Black Company began it from the ranks; Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire made it commercial; Abercrombie's First Law is the form's stylistic summit, its endings systematically refusing redemption; Erikson's Malazan runs it at civilizational scale with compassion intact.
entries.application: Ambiguity must be earned through characterization rather than asserted by body count — the failure mode is nihilism-as-texture, where cruelty substitutes for consequence. Give the book at least one value it takes seriously, so the darkness has something to press against. Price victories honestly: what the protagonists lose should be legible to the reader who wanted them to win.

entries.name: Low Fantasy
entries.description: Magic rationed to a whisper — a world whose physics the reader can mostly trust.
entries.principle: The fantastic is rare, unreliable, or ambiguous, and the story runs on human problems — politics, survival, crime, war — with magic as pressure rather than solution. The contract is grounding: because the reader can predict most of the world, each intrusion of the impossible lands with disproportionate force.
entries.example: Martin's Westeros runs low through its early volumes (magic's return is itself the plot); Abercrombie keeps wizards marginal and suspect; Kay's historical fantasies — Tigana, The Lions of Al-Rassan — hold the magic to a quarter-turn from real history.
entries.application: Set the exchange rate early — how much magic, how visible, at what cost — and hold it; drifting upward in later volumes breaks the ground the form stands on. Because wonder is scarce, spend it deliberately: one genuinely impossible thing, well placed, outperforms an ambient supply. The craft weight shifts onto politics and character, so build both to literary standard.

entries.name: Fantasy of Manners
entries.description: Swordplay and social maneuver in a mannered secondary world — the drawing room with duels.
entries.principle: The comedy of manners and the intrigue novel transplanted into invented cities: rank, reputation, wit, and marriage politics carry the plot, magic is minimal or absent, and the duel replaces the battle. Its pleasure is legibility — the reader learns a class system, then watches characters exploit it with precision.
entries.example: Kushner's Swordspoint defined the form; Stevermer and Wrede's Sorcery & Cecelia runs the epistolary Regency variant; Clarke's Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell carries it at novel-of-manners length with footnotes doing the worldbuilding.
entries.application: Build the social code first and make its violations legible — a cut direct must be as dangerous as a drawn blade, and the reader has to feel why. Wit is load-bearing: dialogue carries plot the way action does in epic, so the sentences have to be genuinely good. The border with Regency romance and gaslamp is porous; decide whether magic exists at all before drafting, because that single answer sets the register.

entries.name: Military Fantasy
entries.description: The campaign from inside the ranks: logistics, command, and the soldier's-eye view of the epic.
entries.principle: War is the subject rather than the backdrop — supply lines, morale, orders that make no sense from below, and professional competence as the source of both tension and identity. Magic functions as a weapons system with doctrine, cost, and countermeasures, which is precisely what separates the form from epic's set-piece battles.
entries.example: Cook's The Black Company narrates from the company annals; Erikson's Malazan — written by an archaeologist-anthropologist — runs the form at continental scale; Wexler's Shadow Campaigns applies Napoleonic drill to a flintlock setting; Abercrombie's The Heroes compresses it to a single three-day battle.
entries.application: Research a real military system and translate it — ranks, drill, logistics, the paperwork — because readers who have served will feel the gap immediately. Give magic doctrine: if it can be countered it can be tactical, and if it cannot, your battle is a rout with dialogue. The unit is this form's found family, and the roster must be allowed to shrink.

entries.name: Dying Earth
entries.description: The far future or deep decadence, where magic is the residue of forgotten science and everything is late.
entries.principle: Entropy as premise: civilizations have already peaked, the sun is dimming, and protagonists scavenge among ruins whose technology reads as sorcery. The register is baroque, ironic, and melancholy; the reader is promised strangeness and the specific pleasure of a world too old to explain itself.
entries.example: Vance's The Dying Earth founded it — and handed D&D its spell system; Wolfe's The Book of the New Sun is the literary summit, narrated by an unreliable torturer with a perfect memory; Harrison's Viriconium deconstructs the mode; Elden Ring carries its aesthetic into games.
entries.application: Withhold explanation as a discipline — the reader should feel the weight of lost time rather than be briefed on it. Vocabulary is a primary instrument: Wolfe used archaic real words rather than invented ones, and the prose reads excavated rather than coined. Keep the irony, too; the form curdles into ordinary post-apocalypse the moment it takes its own ruins solemnly.

entries.name: Dark Fantasy
entries.description: Fantasy operating at horror's temperature: dread, monstrosity, and wonder that bites.
entries.principle: The border form where fantasy's furniture — magic, monsters, secondary worlds — is aimed at fear rather than consolation, while the story keeps fantasy's shape (a quest, a bargain, a world with rules) rather than horror's (an intrusion, a survival). Beauty and dread are held together: the magic is genuinely magical and genuinely wrong.
entries.example: Barker's Weaveworld and Cabal; Gaiman's Sandman at its darkest and Carey's Lucifer; Bardugo's Ninth House; the Souls games' aesthetic; Kingfisher's What Moves the Dead for the modern short form.
entries.application: Keep the fantasy contract — rules, worldbuilding, a protagonist with agency — or you have written horror with elves. Dread here is generated by cost and inevitability rather than gore, and a bargain the reader can see closing is the most reliable engine available. The horror pack will cover fear's mechanics in depth; treat this card as the crossing point rather than the whole territory.

entries.name: Weird Fiction / New Weird
entries.description: Genre boundaries dissolved on purpose: the fantastic as estrangement rather than comfort.
entries.principle: The Weird refuses both the reassuring monster and the tidy secondary world — its creatures resist classification, its cities are baroque and political, its metaphysics are deliberately unresolvable. The New Weird added urban density, materialist politics, and an eye for economy and labor, positioning itself explicitly against the pastoral Tolkien inheritance.
entries.example: Hodgson and Lovecraft supply the old Weird's cosmic strain, the latter's politics to be interrogated rather than inherited; Mieville's Perdido Street Station launched the New Weird; VanderMeer's Annihilation and Harrison's late work run its literary wing.
entries.application: Resist taxonomy — the moment your impossible thing acquires a stat block, you have left the Weird for epic. Build cities and economies rather than kingdoms; the form's politics are structural rather than decorative. And accept the trade honestly: irresolution costs you readers who want a system, and buys a strangeness no system can produce.

entries.name: Gothic Fantasy
entries.description: The haunted house scaled to a world: inheritance, decay, and a past that refuses burial.
entries.principle: Gothic machinery — the cursed lineage, the labyrinthine house, the buried crime, the figure in the corridor — run in a setting where the supernatural is literal rather than suspected. The architecture functions as the antagonist's body, the plot is an excavation, and the past's claim on the present is the permanent theme.
entries.example: Peake's Gormenghast is the form's cathedral, a castle so vast it constitutes a world; Clarke's Piranesi runs it as metaphysical labyrinth; Moreno-Garcia's Mexican Gothic and Bardugo's Ninth House carry the contemporary strain.
entries.application: Make the building a system — routes, rooms, rules, rituals — so that exploration is plot rather than atmosphere. The inheritance question (who owns this, and what was done to acquire it) is the most reliable engine the form offers. Register matters: here the note is decay and grandeur rather than terror, and the ending is typically a reckoning rather than an escape.

entries.name: Urban Fantasy
entries.description: Magic in the contemporary city, hidden behind the world we already know.
entries.principle: The masquerade is the engine — a supernatural society operating inside modern institutions, with rules about exposure that generate plot at every turn. The city is rendered with journalistic specificity precisely so the magic has something solid to violate; the register runs from noir procedural to romance depending on what the protagonist does for a living.
entries.example: de Lint supplies the mythic-urban roots; Butcher's Dresden Files runs the private-investigator variant; Hamilton and Harris built the paranormal-romance wing; Gaiman's Neverwhere and Aaronovitch's Rivers of London mark the London school's poles; Okorafor's Akata Witch and Older's Shadowshaper relocate the form entirely.
entries.application: Pick your masquerade rule and enforce it — who knows, what happens when the veil slips, and why the state has not solved this already. Real-city specificity is the authenticity currency: name streets, transit lines, and neighbourhoods correctly, because local readers are your loudest advocates or critics. The border with paranormal romance is a tone decision made in chapter one, never a late pivot.

entries.name: Portal Fantasy
entries.description: A door from our world into another — and the question of what returning costs.
entries.principle: The reader's surrogate crosses over, which conveniently solves exposition (the protagonist must be told things) and creates the form's real subject: the relationship between the two worlds. The strongest entries put their weight on the return — what the traveller brings back, or cannot bring back, or cannot stop wanting.
entries.example: Carroll and Baum founded it; Lewis's Narnia fixed the children's template; Pullman's His Dark Materials made the multiverse theological; McGuire's Wayward Children and Novik's Scholomance interrogate the tradition directly, asking what happens to the children who come home.
entries.application: Decide the return policy before drafting — one-way, revolving, or costly — because it determines the ending's entire shape. The newcomer's ignorance is your exposition budget: spend it early, then let them become competent. YA/MG expression: this is the form's native habitat, and the modern current runs on aftermath — the child who returns changed, disbelieved, or unable to stay — which gives very old machinery genuine emotional stakes.

entries.name: Historical Fantasy
entries.description: The documented past, with the magic that people at the time actually believed in.
entries.principle: Real history is the substrate, and the fantastic enters either as the period's own beliefs made literal — saints, witches, the fae, the evil eye — or as a divergence the plot must then honour rigorously. The contract is dual: period accuracy for everything the magic does not touch, and real consequence for everything it does.
entries.example: Kay's Tigana and Under Heaven run a quarter-turn from real history; Clarke's Jonathan Strange puts magic into the Napoleonic wars with footnoted scholarship; Novik's Temeraire adds dragons to the same conflict and follows the logistics honestly; Chakraborty's Daevabad draws on Islamic-world history and folklore.
entries.application: Research to the point where you can decide what your magic displaces — if dragons exist, cavalry doctrine changes, and readers will check. Kay's serial-numbers-filed approach (a world clearly Byzantium but not Byzantium) buys freedom at the cost of recognition; choose deliberately rather than drifting. Period belief systems remain the richest source of magic that feels native rather than imported.

entries.name: Gaslamp Fantasy
entries.description: Victorian and Edwardian settings where magic is a science, a scandal, or a profession.
entries.principle: The nineteenth century's institutions — societies, journals, clubs, empires, the newly professionalized sciences — applied to magic, so the fantastic becomes bureaucratized: papers are read, credentials disputed, practitioners feud in print. The aesthetic is gaslight and manners; the machinery is institutional, and the conflicts are about respectability as much as power.
entries.example: Clarke's Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell is the masterwork, magic revived as an English profession complete with academic rivalry; Carriger's Parasol Protectorate runs the comic wing; the steampunk adjacency supplies the technological variant.
entries.application: Institutionalize the magic — who trains, who licenses, who publishes — because the period's obsession with standing is your conflict engine. Empire is unavoidable in these settings, so decide whether the book interrogates it or merely decorates with it; readers will notice either way. Register is everything: the prose should carry period cadence without collapsing into pastiche.

entries.name: Flintlock Fantasy
entries.description: Gunpowder, revolution, and industrialization arriving in the secondary world.
entries.principle: The form advances fantasy's default technology from medieval to early modern and takes the consequences seriously: massed infantry beats knights, printing spreads sedition, and the political register shifts from succession to revolution. Magic must contend with the musket, which is simultaneously the subgenre's central design problem and its best source of conflict.
entries.example: McClellan's Powder Mage trilogy named the form; Wexler's Shadow Campaigns runs Napoleonic drill; Sanderson's later Mistborn era deliberately moves a secondary world into industrial modernity; Kuang's The Poppy War carries the register to a twentieth-century analogue with its violence intact.
entries.application: Work out the magic-versus-firearms exchange rate first; if a single mage beats a regiment, you have written epic in costume. Revolution is the native plot — the old order falling to gunpowder and pamphlets — so build a social order genuinely worth toppling. Follow the industrial logic too: gunpowder implies mines, factories, and a working class the story can honestly include.

entries.name: Mythic / Mythopoeic Fantasy
entries.description: Invented legend that behaves as though it were ancient — fantasy written in myth's register.
entries.principle: The mode aims at the feel of inherited story: archetypal figures, elevated diction, cosmological stakes, and structures that echo epic and scripture rather than the novel. The reader is promised resonance rather than realism, and character psychology yields ground to fate, pattern, and meaning.
entries.example: Tolkien's The Silmarillion is the pure case, with his essay "On Fairy-Stories" as manifesto; Le Guin's Earthsea sustains mythic register at novel length; Beagle's The Last Unicorn and Crowley's Little, Big run the lyric wing; the Mythopoeic Awards exist to mark this tradition specifically.
entries.application: Pitch the prose deliberately — register is the form, and a modern colloquial voice will collapse it in a paragraph. Structure by pattern (threes, falls, returns) rather than by three-act plotting. The standing risk is emotional distance, since mythic figures are types; give the reader one character rendered close enough to grieve for.

entries.name: Fairy-Tale Retelling
entries.description: The old tale reopened — inverted, extended, or told from the other side.
entries.principle: The reader arrives already knowing the plot, so suspense lives entirely in interpretation: whose story this really is, what the original elided, and what the tale looks like once its logic is taken seriously. The source's compression is the opportunity — fairy tales are all skeleton, and the retelling supplies flesh, motive, and cost.
entries.example: Carter's The Bloody Chamber is the literary summit, excavating the tales' sexual politics; McKinley's Beauty and Deerskin founded the modern YA current; Novik's Uprooted and Spinning Silver draw on Polish and Jewish folklore; Valente's Deathless works the Russian material.
entries.application: Identify what the original leaves unexplained and build the book precisely there — the motive, the economics, the aftermath. Decide your relationship to the source (honouring, interrogating, inverting), because a retelling that merely retells has no reason to exist. YA expression: the dominant current in YA fantasy, where the form's identity question — who am I inside a story I was handed? — lands with particular force.

entries.name: The Matter of Britain
entries.description: Arthur, Camelot, and the Grail — the West's most-rewritten fantasy cycle.
entries.principle: A shared body of material (Malory's compilation and its medieval sources) that each generation retells to argue about its own politics: kingship, loyalty, faith, and the failure of ideals. Reader foreknowledge is total — Camelot always falls — so the form runs on interpretation, and on which characters receive the interiority the sources denied them.
entries.example: White's The Once and Future King is the modern touchstone, Arthur's education staged as political theory; Bradley's The Mists of Avalon relocated the cycle to its women; Stewart's Merlin trilogy runs the historical-Roman reading; Cornwell's Warlord Chronicles the hard-historical one.
entries.application: Choose your source layer — Welsh myth, Malory's chivalry, Victorian romance, or Dark Ages history — because they are mutually incompatible and readers will place you within a page. Give the tragedy full weight; a Camelot that survives is a different book with different obligations. Fresh entries almost always come from a viewpoint the sources sidelined.

entries.name: Norse & Northern Matter
entries.description: The Eddas and sagas — fated heroes, a doomed pantheon, and courage without hope.
entries.principle: The northern material supplies a distinctive theology (gods who will lose and know it), a distinctive heroism (what Tolkien called the theory of northern courage — fighting on when defeat is certain), and a saga prose register that is itself a craft resource: laconic, genealogical, and matter-of-fact about violence.
entries.example: The Eddas and Icelandic sagas are the source; Tolkien's entire legendarium is downstream of them, from dwarf names to Ragnarök's shadow; Gaiman's Norse Mythology and American Gods carry the modern retelling; the God of War games shape the current popular image.
entries.application: The saga voice — understatement, feud logic, lineage — is the tradition's most portable tool, and worth trying before reaching for elevated mythic register. Fate is the theme, so build a doom the characters can see approaching and let them choose it anyway. Know the reception history too: this material has been claimed by extremist movements, and a serious book should be aware of what it is taking back.

entries.name: Celtic & Otherworld Matter
entries.description: The fae, the hollow hills, and the bargain you cannot safely refuse.
entries.principle: The Irish, Welsh, and Scottish traditions supply an Otherworld adjacent to ours rather than above it — reachable, dangerous, and governed by rules of hospitality, debt, and exact wording. The distinctive engine is the bargain: the fae cannot lie but will ruin you with the truth, and time runs differently on the other side.
entries.example: The Mabinogion and the Irish cycles are the source; Alexander's Prydain and Cooper's The Dark Is Rising taught generations of readers; Kay's Fionavar and Marillier's Sevenwaters run the epic wing; the contemporary fae-romance current (Black, Maas) descends directly from this material.
entries.application: Make the rules of exchange explicit, then enforce them ruthlessly — the tension is entirely contractual, and a bargain the author fudges kills the form. Time slippage is the tradition's best structural device; use it to impose cost rather than to solve plot problems. Treat the source cultures as living rather than antique: this material belongs to nations with current literatures and firm opinions about its use.

entries.name: Wuxia
entries.description: The Chinese martial-heroes tradition: itinerant swordsmen, sworn brotherhood, and the jianghu's own code.
entries.principle: A centuries-old vernacular tradition rather than a fantasy subgenre borrowed into English. Martial artists move through the jianghu — the "rivers and lakes" world outside official society — governed by xia, a chivalric ethic of righteousness, loyalty, and vengeance, with martial ability heightened but, in the strictest forms, not supernatural.
entries.example: Jin Yong's novels are the canon (Legend of the Condor Heroes, The Smiling, Proud Wanderer) and are now widely translated; Gu Long supplies the terser, noirish strain; Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon and Hero carry the cinematic register to global audiences.
entries.application: Read in translation before writing in the register — the tradition has its own structures (sect politics, secret manuals, master-disciple debts) that a sword-and-sorcery frame will mangle on contact. The moral vocabulary is the point: xia is not knighthood and the jianghu is not an underworld. Anglophone writers should be explicit, to themselves and in the book's apparatus, about whether they are writing within the tradition or adjacent to it.

entries.name: Xianxia & Cultivation
entries.description: Immortal seekers ascending through cultivation — the Daoist-inflected fantasy driving global web fiction.
entries.principle: Where wuxia is martial and human-scaled, xianxia is explicitly supernatural: practitioners cultivate qi through named stages toward immortality, with sects, tribulations, and a cosmology drawn from Daoist and Buddhist frameworks. The progression structure — measurable advancement through defined realms — is both the form's engine and its most successful export.
entries.example: The web-novel platforms built the modern scale; Mo Xiang Tong Xiu's Grandmaster of Demonic Cultivation carried it to Anglophone readers via translation and animation; the danmei wing brought much of that audience; Western progression fantasy descends from these structures directly.
entries.application: The realm ladder is a structural contract — readers track advancement closely, so define the stages and honour them without exception. Understand the religious substrate before borrowing: cultivation is a fictionalization of real practice rather than a magic system invented for novels. Note the serialized economics too — chapter-a-day publishing shapes the pacing, and print structure requires deliberate rebalancing.

entries.name: Silkpunk
entries.description: East Asian materials and aesthetics driving a technology-forward secondary world.
entries.principle: Ken Liu's coinage for a fantasy engineering vocabulary built from bamboo, silk, paper, and sinew rather than brass and steam — a deliberate corrective to the assumption that fantastic technology must look Victorian. The politics are equally deliberate: the form draws on Chinese historical narrative and its own literary conventions rather than Western medievalism.
entries.example: Ken Liu's Dandelion Dynasty, beginning with The Grace of Kings, named and defined it; Chakraborty and Kuang work adjacent territory from different sources; Zhao's Iron Widow runs a YA-facing mecha variant.
entries.application: Let materials dictate machines — an airship of silk and bamboo behaves differently from one of iron, and that difference is the aesthetic's entire argument. Study the source narrative traditions, particularly the Chinese historical epic's approach to time, cast size, and moral judgment, rather than importing Western epic structure with new set dressing. Attribution matters: name your sources in the afterword.

entries.name: Afro-Fantasy & Diaspora Traditions
entries.description: African and diasporic mythologies, histories, and futures rendered as fantasy on their own terms.
entries.principle: A rapidly expanding body of work drawing on West African, East African, and diasporic material — Yoruba and Igbo cosmologies, Ethiopian and Malian history, Caribbean folk practice — that declines the tradition's default medieval-European frame. The stakes are frequently and explicitly historical: slavery, colonialism, and their afterlives handled inside fantastic structures.
entries.example: Okorafor's Who Fears Death and Akata Witch, framed by her Africanfuturism argument; Adeyemi's Children of Blood and Bone in YA; Clark's Dead Djinn universe; James's Black Leopard, Red Wolf drawing on African epic traditions; Hopkinson's Caribbean-rooted work.
entries.application: Specificity beats "African" as a category — the continent holds thousands of traditions with incompatible cosmologies, and readers from them will know immediately. Research source practice as living religion where it is one. For writers outside these traditions the standard is consultation, credit, and a clear answer to why this material and why you.

entries.name: Magical Realism
entries.description: The impossible treated as unremarkable — a literary mode with its own history, frequently miscalled fantasy.
entries.principle: The defining move is narrative affect: the fantastic occurs and nobody, the narration included, treats it as strange. It emerged as a specific movement — Latin American, mid-century, politically engaged — in which the impossible carries historical trauma and official lies made literal. It sits here as a border card because English-language marketing has stretched the term far past its origins.
entries.example: García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude is the canonical case; Rulfo, Allende, and Borges (adjacent) supply the tradition; Okri and Rushdie carry it into postcolonial contexts; Morrison's Beloved runs American material through comparable technique.
entries.application: If you want the mode rather than the label, the technique is flatness — the impossible reported in the same register as weather, with no character pausing to marvel. Understand what you are borrowing: applying the term to any whimsical contemporary fantasy erases a specific political literature. When uncertain, describe your book's actual mechanics rather than reaching for the prestige term.

entries.name: Romantasy
entries.description: Romance structure and fantasy setting at equal weight — the market's dominant current form.
entries.principle: A true hybrid rather than fantasy with a love story: the romance's genre obligations (the couple as the plot's spine, the emotional beat structure, an HEA or HFN ending) are binding alongside the fantasy's worldbuilding and stakes. Failing either contract fails the book, which is why the form is considerably harder to execute than its sales figures suggest.
entries.example: Maas's A Court of Thorns and Roses and Throne of Glass built the modern readership; Yarros's Fourth Wing took it to record commercial scale; Bardugo, Black, and Chakraborty run adjacent territory; fae-bargain and dragon-rider premises dominate the current market.
entries.application: Learn romance beats properly — the meet, the forced proximity, the black moment, the grovel, the resolution — because romance readers will grade you on them and fantasy instincts will sabotage the pacing. The magic system should generate romantic obstacles (bonds, bargains, mated pairs) rather than sitting politely beside them. YA note: much of this readership crossed over from YA, and the boundary is a content-and-voice decision worth making explicitly rather than by drift.

entries.name: Cozy Fantasy
entries.description: Low stakes by design: the coffee shop, the bakery, the retired adventurer's second act.
entries.principle: A reassurance contract — the reader is promised that nothing irreversible will happen, and the engine becomes craft, community, and small problems solved kindly. It emerged as an explicit counter-current to grimdark, and its rules are every bit as binding: cruelty, gore, and existential threat break the form outright.
entries.example: Baldree's Legends & Lattes defined the modern wave with an orc opening a coffee shop; Klune's The House in the Cerulean Sea preceded it in temperament; Kingfisher's baking-adjacent books and the Studio Ghibli register are the tonal ancestors.
entries.application: Replace threat with want — the business that might fail, the relationship not yet spoken, the recipe not yet right — and take those wants seriously enough to carry a novel. Competence and craft detail are the form's central pleasure, so render the work itself in loving specificity. Hold the register absolutely: a single genuine atrocity voids the contract the reader paid for.

entries.name: Comic Fantasy
entries.description: The genre laughing at itself — satire, parody, and jokes with structural integrity.
entries.principle: The form works by taking a fantasy premise entirely seriously and following it to absurd but rigorous conclusions; the best entries are simultaneously the funniest and the most humane. Parody alone dates quickly, which is why the tradition's survivors are the ones carrying a moral argument underneath the jokes.
entries.example: Pratchett's Discworld is the summit, satire that grew into the genre's ethical conscience; Adams supplies the adjacent science-fiction register; Anthony's Xanth marks the pun-driven strain; Kingfisher's comic wing continues it.
entries.application: Build jokes on worldbuilding logic rather than references — "what if a city genuinely had a Thieves' Guild with a budget and a complaints procedure" outlasts a Tolkien gag by decades. Comic form permits real anger: Pratchett's method was moral fury delivered as farce. Structure the book straight, too, since a comedy that abandons plot discipline stops being funny somewhere around the midpoint.

entries.name: Progression Fantasy & LitRPG
entries.description: Measurable advancement as the story's spine — levels, ranks, and systems the reader can track.
entries.principle: The contract is progression itself: a protagonist who visibly and quantifiably grows stronger, with rules explicit enough that the reader can anticipate and audit each advance. LitRPG makes the game layer literal (stats, screens, classes); progression fantasy generalizes it to cultivation ladders and skill trees.
entries.example: The xianxia web novels supply the template; Wight's Cradle is the Anglophone standard-bearer; Dungeon Crawler Carl brought the LitRPG wing to mainstream bestseller lists; the serialized platforms drive the form's economics and its pacing.
entries.application: Publish the rules and never break them — this readership plays the system alongside the protagonist, and an unearned power-up is the cardinal sin. Escalation must stay legible: each tier needs a distinct capability and a distinct new problem. The serialized origins shape rhythm (a beat per chapter), so print-length revision usually means cutting grind rather than adding incident.

entries.name: Animal Fantasy & Beast Fable
entries.description: Animals as protagonists — societies, quests, and mortality at the scale of the warren, the hedge, or the abbey.
entries.principle: The tradition runs from Aesop to full secondary-world epics with animal casts, and its distinctive tension is the balance between real animal behaviour and human-legible society. The strongest entries use the animal frame to write about mortality, migration, and hierarchy with a directness that a human cast would soften.
entries.example: Adams's Watership Down is the summit — rabbit ethology, an invented language and mythology, and a genuinely frightening politics; Jacques's Redwall built the long-running middle-grade franchise; O'Brien's Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH runs the science-adjacent variant; Ghibli's Pom Poko carries the screen wing.
entries.application: Set the anthropomorphism dial early — full clothes-and-castles, or biology-first with only language granted — and hold it, because the middle ground reads as inconsistency. Real ethology is the richest available resource: Watership Down's warren politics and invented Lapine both come from field research. YA/MG expression: this is the tradition's largest readership, and its licence to handle death honestly is precisely why the best of these books last for generations.

entries.name: Magic-System Design: Hard and Soft
entries.description: The genre's foundational choice: magic the reader can reason with, or magic they can only wonder at.
entries.principle: Hard magic has stated rules, so it can solve problems without cheating; soft magic withholds them, so it can generate wonder and dread but must never resolve the plot. The axis is not quality but function — the reader's ability to anticipate what magic can do is exactly proportional to your licence to use it as a tool rather than a mood.
entries.example: Sanderson's Allomancy is the hard pole, costed and enumerated until readers solve fights ahead of the characters; Tolkien's Gandalf is the soft pole, his power never inventoried, which is why his interventions feel like grace rather than mechanics; Le Guin's true-name magic sits between, ruled but rendered in a moral rather than technical register.
entries.application: Decide which end you occupy before drafting, and let it dictate your climaxes: hard-magic endings are solved by cleverness the reader can audit, soft-magic endings by character choice, sacrifice, or grace. Mixing is legitimate but must be zoned — hard rules for the protagonist's toolkit, soft mystery at the world's edges — so the reader always knows which register a scene is operating in.

entries.name: Sanderson's Laws — and the Soft-Magic Counterargument
entries.description: The genre's most-quoted design heuristics, and the tradition that rejects them.
entries.principle: The three laws in brief: your ability to solve conflict with magic is proportional to how well the reader understands it; limitations are more interesting than powers; expand what you have before adding something new. The counterargument, older and equally valid, is that magic's literary function is estrangement — the numinous cannot be spreadsheeted, and a fully explained system stops being magic and becomes physics with robes.
entries.example: Sanderson's Mistborn and Stormlight are the laws demonstrated at industrial scale; the counter-tradition runs from Tolkien through Le Guin to Susanna Clarke, whose English magic is scholarly yet finally unknowable; Miéville has argued the systematized approach domesticates precisely what fantasy exists to unsettle.
entries.application: Treat the laws as tools for one job — plot-solving magic — not as a universal standard. If your book's magic exists to generate awe, dread, or theological weight, the laws will actively damage it. Ask what you want readers to feel when magic appears (cleverness, terror, grief, awe) and adopt the design philosophy that produces that feeling.

entries.name: Cost, Source, and Limit
entries.description: The three questions that turn a power into a system.
entries.principle: Every functioning magic answers three things: where the power comes from, what it costs the user, and what it cannot do. Cost creates drama (the price paid is the scene's stakes), source creates politics (whoever controls it controls the world), and limit creates plot (the problem magic can't solve is the story). Systems that skip any of the three drift toward wish fulfilment.
entries.example: Mistborn's metals are source, ingestion is limit, and burning them is cost — a complete triangle; Fullmetal Alchemist's equivalent exchange makes cost the entire moral engine; the Wheel of Time makes source political by gendering it, so who may touch power is a civilizational conflict rather than a rule.
entries.application: Write the three answers in one paragraph before you write a magical scene, and make the cost visible on the page — physical, moral, or social — every single time magic is used. Then interrogate the source politically: if magic is scarce, someone has monopolized it; if it is universal, your society's economy and warfare should look nothing like medieval Europe's.

entries.name: The Worldbuilding Iceberg
entries.description: Build ten times what you show, then show the tenth that carries weight.
entries.principle: The impression of depth comes from consistency and implication rather than disclosure — readers feel a world's mass through offhand references, unexplained customs, and characters who take their own history for granted. What you build but never state still shapes what you write, because it makes your details cohere.
entries.example: Tolkien's appendices, calendars, and languages exist so that a passing reference to the Second Age carries genuine weight; Le Guin implies the entire Archipelago through a raft, a fog, and a handful of customs; Martin's genealogies inform succession disputes readers only partly follow, and that partial comprehension is what makes Westeros feel real.
entries.application: Build the substructure — histories, languages, economies — then apply the tenth rule ruthlessly at the sentence level: characters reference the past without explaining it, and the narration declines to gloss. The test is whether cut material still constrains the draft; if deleting your invented history would change nothing on the page, you built decoration rather than an iceberg.

entries.name: Invented Language: Use and Abuse
entries.description: A little conlang goes a very long way, and a lot of it goes badly.
entries.principle: Invented language works when it is systematic (a real phonology and a consistent orthography) and rationed (a handful of terms readers can absorb). Its function is texture and cognitive estrangement — a word with no English equivalent implies a concept the culture has and we do not — but every untranslated term is a small tax on comprehension.
entries.example: Tolkien built the languages first and the world to house them, and still put almost none of it in the prose; Adams's Lapine in Watership Down is perhaps thirty words doing enormous work; Herbert's Dune supplies the SF comparison, its glossary carrying weight the novel earns. The failure mode is the fantasy novel opening with three apostrophe-laden names in one sentence.
entries.application: Cap yourself at roughly a dozen invented terms a reader must retain, and introduce each in a context that teaches its meaning without a glossary lookup. Build a consistent sound system even if you invent nothing else, because inconsistent phonology reads as sloppiness even to readers who cannot name why. Apostrophes are not a language.

entries.name: The Map Decision
entries.description: Whether to include one, and what including one promises.
entries.principle: A frontispiece map is a genre signal and a contract: it promises travel, scale, and a story whose geography matters. It also constrains you — readers will measure distances, question why the army marched that way, and notice that your continent has no plausible rainfall. Omitting the map signals intimacy, mystery, or a story where place is psychological rather than logistical.
entries.example: Tolkien drew the map first and let it govern the journey's pacing; Sanderson's maps carry ecological and political information; Clarke's Jonathan Strange has no map because its geography is England's, and Piranesi's absence of one is the whole point.
entries.application: If you include a map, do the physical geography honestly — mountains create rain shadows, rivers run to the sea, cities sit on trade routes and fresh water — because the readers who care are the ones who evangelize. If you omit it, keep travel vague and psychological rather than tallying days on the road. Either way, decide before drafting, since the choice changes how you write every journey.

entries.name: Secondary-World Exposition
entries.description: Delivering a world the reader has never seen without stopping the story to lecture.
entries.principle: The problem is unique to invented settings: the reader needs information the viewpoint character considers too obvious to think about. The working solutions are conflict-carried exposition (facts delivered while characters argue about them), the newcomer or outsider viewpoint, the incidental detail that implies structure, and disciplined withholding — trusting readers to tolerate confusion for a chapter.
entries.example: Herbert's Dune deploys epigraph documents so the narrative never pauses; Le Guin lets custom emerge through action; Erikson's Malazan drops readers in with no orientation at all, which costs him readers at chapter one and earns fanaticism from those who stay; Lewis uses the portal newcomer, the oldest solution.
entries.application: Never let a character explain something they would already know to someone who also knows it. Convert exposition into disagreement wherever possible — two characters with different stakes in the same fact will explain it while fighting about it. And measure your withholding tolerance honestly against your target reader: literary and epic audiences will wait, commercial and YA audiences want orientation fast.

entries.name: Names and Naming
entries.description: Nomenclature is the reader's first and most constant contact with your world.
entries.principle: Names do three jobs — they signal culture (names from one people should share sound patterns), they carry connotation through phonaesthetics, and they must be pronounceable enough to survive being read silently for four hundred pages. A cast whose names are mutually unpronounceable or visually similar creates a comprehension tax that compounds across a series.
entries.example: Tolkien, a philologist, built naming systems where etymology encodes history; Le Guin's Earthsea names are short and vowel-clean, so a hundred islands stay distinct; the common failure is the epic whose eight lords are Kaelen, Kaelor, Kalen, and Kaelith.
entries.application: Build two or three sound palettes for your major cultures and stay inside them, so readers can place a stranger by their name alone. Vary first letters and syllable counts across your principal cast for scannability. Say every name aloud, and cut anything you cannot pronounce twice the same way — readers subvocalize, and a name they stumble over becomes a name they skim.

entries.name: Deep Time and Layered History
entries.description: Making a world feel older and larger than the story you are telling in it.
entries.principle: Depth comes from stratification: ruins whose builders are forgotten, words whose meanings have drifted, grudges nobody can source, and religions that have already schismed twice. The effect requires that your world's past be uneven — some ages documented, some lost, some deliberately misremembered — because uniform history reads as an encyclopedia rather than a civilization.
entries.example: Tolkien's Third Age rests visibly on the ruins of the Second; Wolfe's Urth is layered so deeply that its magic is our forgotten technology; Erikson's archaeological training shows in Malazan's stacked civilizations; Elden Ring tells its entire history through item descriptions and architecture.
entries.application: Write a timeline with deliberate gaps and at least one official lie, then let characters disagree about the past according to who benefits. Physical stratification is the cheapest tool available — a newer wall built on an older foundation implies a thousand years in one sentence. Keep the reader slightly less informed than the scholars in the book, and the world will feel bottomless.

entries.name: The Consequence Cascade
entries.description: Pick one hard constraint and follow it everywhere it goes.
entries.principle: The most convincing invented worlds are usually generated rather than assembled: a single premise — a climate, a magic, a biological fact — propagated rigorously into architecture, agriculture, religion, art, and law until the culture could not plausibly be otherwise. Consistency of derivation reads as authenticity in a way that accumulated detail never does.
entries.example: Sanderson's Roshar begins with world-crossing highstorms and derives crustacean biology, leeward cities, retracting plants, and storm-based religion; Herbert derives an entire ecology and theology from Arrakis's water scarcity; Jemisin's Broken Earth builds culture, caste, and architecture from seismic catastrophe.
entries.application: Choose your one premise early and then run it through a checklist of domains — food, shelter, war, worship, art, trade, childrearing, death — asking what changes in each. When two derived facts conflict, resolve rather than ignore, because the resolution usually generates your best material. Resist adding a second unrelated premise until the first is exhausted.

entries.name: Quest Structure
entries.description: The genre's oldest architecture, and how to keep it from becoming a checklist.
entries.principle: The quest supplies natural forward motion, episodic variety, and a physical metaphor for internal change — but it fails when the journey becomes a sequence of encounters rather than an accumulating transformation. Each stage must cost the party something they cannot regain, so arrival is not merely geographic.
entries.example: The Lord of the Rings paces its stages so the Fellowship's fracture is the middle's real event; Alexander's Prydain runs the shape for younger readers with the loss made explicit; the tabletop-influenced failure mode is the novel that reads as a sequence of encounters between inns.
entries.application: Chart what the journey takes as well as what it covers — a companion, an illusion, a capability — so the party arriving is measurably poorer or altered. Give the destination a complication known in advance, so anticipation does structural work. And vary the encounter types deliberately: negotiation, endurance, temptation, and grief should appear alongside combat, or the middle turns monotonous.

entries.name: Prophecy Plotting Without Determinism
entries.description: The genre's most abused device, and the ways to make it carry tension rather than remove it.
entries.principle: Prophecy's problem is that guaranteed outcomes drain suspense; its solutions are ambiguity (the words fit multiple futures), cost (the prophecy is accurate but the price is unstated), agency (the characters fulfil it through choices that feel free), and subversion (the prophecy is wrong, manipulated, or self-fulfilling because people acted on it).
entries.example: Macbeth is still the model for the self-fulfilling variant, where acting on the prophecy causes it; Herbert's Dune treats prophecy as engineered propaganda, the Bene Gesserit having seeded the legend that traps Paul; Rowling's chosen-one prophecy is explicitly activated by the villain's decision to act on it.
entries.application: Write the prophecy after you know your ending, then work backwards to phrasing that is honest yet misdirecting — the reader should be able to re-read it and see that it never lied. Make characters' belief in it a plot force independent of its truth. If your prophecy simply announces what will happen and then it happens, cut it and lose nothing.

entries.name: The Chosen One, Handled
entries.description: The most exhausted premise in the genre, and why it keeps working anyway.
entries.principle: Chosenness offers instant stakes and a reader-flattering identification, and costs agency — if destiny drives the plot, the protagonist's choices are decoration. The functional versions convert the trope into a burden (chosenness as trauma), a fraud (chosenness as manufactured), a collective (many chosen, or the wrong one), or a starting point rather than a resolution.
entries.example: Le Guin's Ged is gifted rather than chosen, and his gift is the problem; Jordan's Rand is crushed by the prophecy that empowers him; Abercrombie and the grimdark wing systematically deflate the trope; Fitz in Hobb's Farseer books is chosen into servitude rather than glory.
entries.application: If you use it, make the protagonist's choices matter more than their status — the ending should turn on a decision only this person would make, not a power only this person has. Consider giving chosenness a political history: who declared it, who benefits, and what happens to the ones passed over. And check whether your premise still works if the prophecy is deleted; if it does, the story is stronger without it.

entries.name: Multi-POV Epic Management
entries.description: Running six to sixty viewpoints without losing the reader or the thread.
entries.principle: Multi-POV buys scale, dramatic irony, and the ability to show a war from three sides; it costs momentum at every switch and risks the reader skimming toward their favourite. The discipline is that each viewpoint needs its own want, arc, and distinct voice, and each chapter must advance the whole book rather than merely maintaining its thread.
entries.example: Martin runs named-character chapters with cliffhanger turns to survive the switch cost; Erikson escalates to dozens of viewpoints and accepts the reader attrition; Sanderson uses interludes to widen scope without diluting his principals; Jordan's mid-series bloat is the canonical cautionary case.
entries.application: Audit for the skim test: if any viewpoint could be summarized in a paragraph without loss, fold it. Stagger your threads so at least one is always at high tension. And converge on schedule — readers will tolerate separation for a long time provided the book demonstrates, periodically, that the strands are approaching each other.

entries.name: Series Architecture at Ten Books
entries.description: Planning a long fantasy series so that the middle has a reason to exist.
entries.principle: Long series fail in predictable ways: the middle sags because the endpoint was never fixed, the cast bloats because new viewpoints are easier than resolving old ones, and the escalation outruns the world's ability to raise stakes credibly. The corrective is an architecture decided early — the endpoint, the arc-per-volume, and what each book resolves as well as advances.
entries.example: Jordan's Wheel of Time is the field's most-studied case of both ambition and mid-series drift; Sanderson's Stormlight has published its ten-book architecture including a mid-series time skip; Hobb structures trilogies-within-a-larger-arc so each cluster closes; Pratchett's Discworld avoids the problem entirely by being standalone-first.
entries.application: Write the last chapter's shape before publishing the first book, even if you never use it. Give every volume a complete internal arc — a question raised and answered — so the series contract is honoured book by book rather than deferred. And decide your cast policy in advance: a series that never retires viewpoints will accumulate them past the reader's carrying capacity.

entries.name: The Trilogy Shape
entries.description: The genre's default container, and what each volume owes.
entries.principle: The functional fantasy trilogy is not one novel in three parts but three novels with escalating scope: book one establishes world, character, and a local victory; book two widens the world, complicates the victory, and typically ends at the arc's lowest point; book three converges and pays every debt. The second book carries the highest failure rate because it must expand without resolving.
entries.example: Sanderson's original Mistborn trilogy is the engineered case, each volume reframing the previous book's victory as a mistake; Hobb's Farseer runs the shape at emotional rather than plot scale; Novik's Scholomance compresses it into a school year each.
entries.application: Give book two its own complete arc rather than treating it as transit — the middle volume needs a question it alone answers. Plant book three's solution in book one, so the ending reads as inevitable rather than arriving. And decide early whether your trilogy is escalating scope or deepening intimacy, since those require opposite structures for volume two.

entries.name: The Standalone Fantasy
entries.description: The single-volume secondary world, and why it is harder than it looks.
entries.principle: A standalone must deliver worldbuilding depth, a complete character arc, and a resolved plot in one volume — which means the world has to be conveyed at speed and the ending must close rather than gesture at sequels. The compensating advantage is enormous: standalone fantasy has a distinct readership, and reviewers and awards favour completeness.
entries.example: Clarke's Jonathan Strange delivers a full alternate history and a resolved rivalry in one book; Kay's Tigana and Under Heaven do it repeatedly; Novik's Uprooted and Spinning Silver are the modern commercial proof; Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea works as a standalone despite its sequels.
entries.application: Narrow the world's aperture — one region, one system, one conflict rendered deeply — rather than sketching a continent you lack room to develop. Let the protagonist's arc and the plot resolve on the same beat, since you have no sequel to distribute them across. And close the ending honestly: the standalone's promise is completeness, and a final-page sequel hook reads as a broken contract.

entries.name: Eucatastrophe and Its Alternatives
entries.description: Tolkien's term for the sudden joyous turn — and the endings the genre has built against it.
entries.principle: Eucatastrophe is the unlooked-for grace at the point of defeat, which Tolkien argued was fantasy's distinctive consolation and its highest function. Its alternatives are the pyrrhic ending (victory at unbearable cost), the ambiguous ending (the world changed but unresolved), and the grimdark refusal (no restoration offered). Each is a different promise, and the reader has been reading for one of them since chapter one.
entries.example: The eagles at the Black Gate, and Sam carrying Frodo, are the term's own examples; Abercrombie systematically inverts it, his endings arriving as bleak reversals; Jemisin's Broken Earth ends with a changed world rather than a restored one; Pratchett tends to eucatastrophe earned by ordinary decency.
entries.application: Identify which ending your book has been promising through its register, and deliver that one — a grimdark novel that resolves in grace reads as a cheat, and a warm quest that ends in ash reads as a betrayal. If you want eucatastrophe, earn it by making the defeat genuine first: the turn only lands when the reader has actually surrendered hope.

entries.name: Battle Scenes at Scale
entries.description: Armies clashing, rendered so the reader knows what is happening and why it matters.
entries.principle: Large battles fail when they become weather — noise without geography, stakes, or comprehensible progress. The functional approach anchors the scale to one viewpoint who can only see a fragment, supplies the reader with the plan beforehand so deviations register, and marks progress through concrete signposts rather than abstract description.
entries.example: Tolkien alternates between Pelennor's panorama and individual encounters so scale and intimacy reinforce each other; Abercrombie's The Heroes runs an entire novel on three days of one battle, viewpoints passing like a baton; Cook's Black Company keeps the camera at squad level throughout.
entries.application: Establish the plan, the terrain, and the objective before the first clash, so the reader can track failure and improvisation. Keep viewpoints low and specific — one soldier's mud and confusion communicates a rout better than a narrator's overview. Mark the turn explicitly: readers need to know the moment the battle's outcome changed, even if the characters do not.

entries.name: The Duel
entries.description: Single combat as character revelation rather than choreography.
entries.principle: A duel's tension comes from what each fighter wants beyond survival and what the outcome will change, not from the sequence of moves. Fantasy adds the question of magical parity: if either combatant can end it instantly, the duel is a formality, so the scene's design work is establishing why they cannot.
entries.example: Kushner's Swordspoint makes duelling a social institution with reputational stakes larger than the blades; Gaiman and Pratchett tend to deflate duels for comic and thematic effect; the wuxia tradition treats combat as philosophical argument between schools.
entries.application: Decide first what the duel decides — status, information, a claim, a marriage — and let that hover over every exchange. Constrain the magic explicitly before the fight so the reader knows the rules being played by. Keep the choreography sparse and the interiority dense: two clear actions and one decision beat outperform a page of parry-riposte.

entries.name: Court Intrigue Mechanics
entries.description: Politics as plot: making conversations carry the tension of combat.
entries.principle: Intrigue needs three things to function — a legible power structure, clear stakes for each player, and information asymmetry the reader can track. The reader must understand who gains what from every move, or the scheming reads as noise; the pleasure is watching a competent player work a system the reader has learned.
entries.example: Martin's small-council scenes are the modern standard, each participant's agenda legible; Kushner's fantasy of manners runs intrigue where a snub is a strike; Kay's Sarantine Mosaic makes court factionalism the entire plot; the Malazan and Dune traditions layer intrigue with prophecy and long games.
entries.application: Draw the org chart and the succession law before writing a single scheme, since intrigue is only comprehensible against a structure. Give each player one thing they want and one thing they fear losing. And let the reader be slightly ahead of at least one character — dramatic irony is intrigue's engine, and total opacity produces confusion rather than suspense.

entries.name: Nonhuman POV
entries.description: Writing minds that are not human without making them humans in costume.
entries.principle: The craft problem is calibration: a viewpoint too alien becomes unreadable, one too familiar wastes the premise. The workable approach differentiates on specific axes — sensory apparatus, lifespan, social structure, moral intuitions — while keeping enough shared ground for the reader to attach. Diction is the primary instrument; how a mind names things reveals what it notices.
entries.example: Adams gives rabbits genuine ethology, an invented language, and a mythology, but keeps their emotions legible; Tchaikovsky's spider viewpoints in Children of Time build cognition from the biology upward; Tolkien's Ents think slowly and speak in a syntax that enacts it; Le Guin's dragons operate on a moral scale that human characters cannot fully access.
entries.application: Pick two or three differences and develop them rigorously rather than gesturing at general alienness — a species that perceives time differently will have different grammar, art, and grief. Let their values be genuinely other, including in ways the reader finds uncomfortable. And use the human characters' misreadings as your exposition device: what they get wrong teaches the reader what is actually there.

entries.name: The Travel Sequence
entries.description: The genre's most common structural dead zone, and how to make the road earn its pages.
entries.principle: Travel is fantasy's default connective tissue and its most reliable source of sag. It earns its length only when it delivers something a scene at either end could not: relationships forged under strain, world revealed by traversal, or resources depleted so later scenes have stakes. Otherwise it is a transition and should be compressed to a sentence.
entries.example: Tolkien uses the road to build the Fellowship and to reveal Middle-earth's stratified history through what they pass; The Wheel of Time's mid-series travel is the standard cautionary case; road narratives outside the genre — pilgrimage structures — supply the models where journey is theme.
entries.application: Give every journey a depletion clock (food, coin, daylight, pursuit) so the road itself applies pressure. Use travel for the conversations that could not happen at court, then cut to arrival the moment those are exhausted. If nothing changes between departure and arrival, write "three weeks later" and move on without apology.

entries.name: Magic in Action Scenes
entries.description: Keeping fights comprehensible when the physics are negotiable.
entries.principle: Magical combat fails when the reader cannot predict the boundaries — if anything might happen, nothing is suspenseful. Comprehensible magical action requires established rules, established costs, and an established reason the fight is not immediately decided, plus geography the reader can hold while the impossible occurs.
entries.example: Sanderson's action scenes are the hard-magic showcase, readers solving the tactical problem alongside the protagonist; Jim Butcher escalates within known limits so each book's finale spends everything established; anime-influenced fights that add new powers mid-battle are the failure case, since escalation without rules is noise.
entries.application: State the constraint in the scene before you break the tension with it — the reader must know the wizard is nearly out of power before the moment that matters. Anchor every magical exchange to a physical consequence: where the bodies are, what broke, who is bleeding. And never introduce a new capability during a climax; if it was not established, it reads as authorial rescue.

entries.name: Wonder: Writing the First Sight
entries.description: The genre's signature emotion, and the technique that produces it.
entries.principle: Wonder is generated by contrast and restraint rather than by adjectives — the reader must feel the ordinary before the extraordinary lands, and the prose must trust a small number of exact details over a catalogue of marvels. The viewpoint character's reaction calibrates the reader's; awe described flatly by an unimpressed narrator will not transmit.
entries.example: Bilbo's first sight of Rivendell and Smaug's hoard work by delay and specificity; Le Guin renders dragons with a handful of details and enormous quiet; Clarke's Piranesi generates continuous wonder from a single unexplained architecture; Ghibli's screen equivalents work by holding on the reaction shot.
entries.application: Establish the mundane baseline first — the more grounded the preceding pages, the higher the wonder registers. Choose three exact details rather than twelve approximate ones, and prefer the unexpected small detail (what it smells like, what it does to sound) over scale. Then let a character be silent, because the pause after the reveal is where the reader's own imagination does your work.

entries.name: The Council Scene
entries.description: The exposition set piece the genre cannot avoid, made bearable.
entries.principle: Fantasy repeatedly needs a scene where informed parties assemble, share what they know, and decide what to do — and that scene is a natural exposition dump with a high risk of inertia. It works when the participants disagree, when the decision is genuinely contested, and when someone in the room is lying or withholding.
entries.example: The Council of Elrond survives its length because every faction has a grievance and a competing claim; Martin's councils are intrigue rather than briefing; the weak version is the scene where allies calmly agree on the quest they were always going to undertake.
entries.application: Give the room at least three incompatible agendas and one secret, so information emerges as ammunition rather than as briefing. Let the decision be genuinely open — if the outcome was inevitable, summarize it. And end the scene on a cost: someone leaves the alliance, someone is overruled, someone resolves privately to betray it.

entries.name: Myth Retelling: Method and Ethics
entries.description: Reworking inherited story, and the questions that come with it.
entries.principle: Retelling trades surprise for resonance: readers know the plot, so the work lives in interpretation, interiority, and what the source suppressed. The ethical dimension varies with the material's status — the Greek and Norse corpora are long-dead religions in the public domain, while living traditions carry obligations of accuracy, respect, and often consultation.
entries.example: Miller's Circe and Song of Achilles give interiority to figures the epics treated as functions; Bradley relocates Arthurian material to its women; Ovid's own Metamorphoses is a reminder that the tradition has always been retold; the failure mode is the retelling that adds nothing but modern dialogue.
entries.application: Identify the source's silence and write there — whose perspective is missing, what is elided, what the tale takes for granted. Decide your relationship to the original before drafting: reverent, corrective, or antagonistic, each of which produces a different book. For living traditions, treat the material as belonging to a current community rather than an archive.

entries.name: Borrowing Across Cultures
entries.description: Using material that is not yours, well.
entries.principle: Fantasy is built on borrowing, and the difference between influence and extraction lies in specificity, research depth, credit, and stakes — whether the source culture is rendered as a living system with its own logic or mined for exotic set dressing. The practical standard the field has converged on is: research to primary sources, consult practitioners where the tradition is living, credit explicitly, and be able to answer why this material and why you.
entries.example: Ken Liu names silkpunk's sources and writes essays about the tradition he draws on; Okorafor distinguishes Africanfuturism from adjacent labels precisely to mark specificity; the field's cautionary cases are the novels that flatten thousands of distinct traditions into a single "eastern" or "African" aesthetic.
entries.application: Go one level deeper than the label — not "Norse" but a specific saga's region and century, not "African" but a named people's cosmology. Pay consultants and credit them in the acknowledgements. And apply the equivalence test: if you would not render your own tradition's sacred practice as decoration, do not do it to someone else's.

entries.name: Medievalism Audited
entries.description: The genre's default setting, and how much of it is actually medieval.
entries.principle: Standard fantasy medievalism is largely a nineteenth-century invention filtered through Victorian romance and twentieth-century wargaming — the real Middle Ages were more mobile, more literate in places, more religiously saturated, more ethnically mixed, and far less uniformly filthy than the genre assumes. Knowing which conventions are historical and which are inherited pastiche is a competitive advantage.
entries.example: Kay and Sansom-adjacent historical fantasy work from real period scholarship; Novik's Temeraire takes Napoleonic logistics seriously; the standing corrective from medievalists is that the all-white, all-Christian, universally squalid medieval Europe of genre convention is not the historical record.
entries.application: Read one serious history of the period you are imitating and let it disrupt at least three of your assumptions — travel, trade, faith, or demography. Ask what your economy actually eats and who grows it, since feudal fantasy usually omits the ninety percent doing agricultural labour. And treat the default as a choice rather than a given: if you keep the conventions, keep them deliberately.

entries.name: Pantheon and Religion in Narrative
entries.description: Gods who exist, and what that does to a society.
entries.principle: Fantasy religion differs from real-world religion in one decisive respect: the gods may be demonstrably real and occasionally present, which changes faith into knowledge and worship into transaction. The interesting work lies in the gap — what the institution teaches versus what the god does, what happens to doubt when miracles are verifiable, and how clergy behave when their employer might answer.
entries.example: Pratchett's Small Gods is the genre's best treatment, belief itself the mechanic; Erikson's Malazan runs ascendancy as a political process; Sanderson's Warbreaker and Elantris make theology structural; Le Guin's Earthsea keeps the numinous impersonal.
entries.application: Decide the gods' actual ontological status and their intervention rate, then derive the institutions from it: a god who answers weekly produces a different priesthood than one silent for a thousand years. Give your religion internal disagreement — schisms, heresies, reformers — because a monolithic faith reads as set dressing. And let ordinary belief be textured: most worshippers in any tradition are casual, syncretic, and inconsistent.

entries.name: Folklore Research for Fiction
entries.description: Working from real folk tradition rather than from other fantasy novels.
entries.principle: Most genre creatures have been filtered through three or four generations of fiction and gaming until little of the original remains — the folkloric fae, for instance, are far stranger, more dangerous, and more locally specific than their genre descendants. Going back to collections, ethnographies, and regional sources yields material nobody else is using.
entries.example: Tolkien worked from philology and the primary corpus rather than from Victorian fairy literature; Novik draws on Polish and Jewish folklore in Uprooted and Spinning Silver; Kingfisher builds from regional folk practice; the contrast is the standard-issue genre elf, three removes from any source.
entries.application: Read the collections and, where available, the ethnographic scholarship rather than encyclopedias of fantasy creatures. Keep the local specificity — a creature from one valley with one rule is more convincing than a species with a stat block. And preserve the strangeness: folklore's inconsistencies and cruelties are exactly what genre sanding has removed, and restoring them is where the fresh material is.

entries.name: Tone Registers: Grimdark to Cozy
entries.description: Setting the emotional contract, and honouring it for four hundred pages.
entries.principle: Fantasy spans the widest tonal range of any genre, from cheerful cozy through mythic solemnity to unrelenting grimdark, and the register is a contract established in the opening pages. Readers forgive dark or light; they do not forgive lurching, because tonal breach reads as authorial incompetence rather than range.
entries.example: Pratchett modulates from farce to genuine grief within a single novel and holds it because the moral seriousness is constant; Abercrombie never once offers unearned comfort; Baldree's cozy register admits mild peril and no atrocity; the failure case is the whimsical opening followed by an unsignalled torture scene.
entries.application: Write your first chapter last if necessary, so it accurately advertises the book's actual register. Test tonal outliers against the contract: a scene of real cruelty in a warm book needs to be either cut or seeded much earlier. And note that darkening across a series is permitted and often effective, provided each volume signals its own temperature honestly.

entries.name: Romantasy Beat Mechanics
entries.description: The romance obligations a fantasy writer must actually learn.
entries.principle: Romance is a structured genre with binding beats, not a subplot: the meeting, the attraction acknowledged, the forced proximity, the deepening, the black moment where the relationship appears lost, the grovel or sacrifice, and the emotionally satisfying resolution. In romantasy these run at equal weight with the fantasy plot, and the two must be braided so that each complicates the other.
entries.example: Maas's series demonstrate the commercial template and the fae-bargain device as obstacle generator; Yarros's Fourth Wing braids the romance beats to a training-and-war structure; Bardugo and Chakraborty run adjacent balances with more worldbuilding weight.
entries.application: Time the black moment against your fantasy climax deliberately — most successful romantasy places the relationship's low point just before the plot's, so the resolution carries both. Generate obstacles from the magic system rather than from misunderstanding, since contrived miscommunication is the form's most-criticized failure. And know the heat level and its conventions before drafting, because it shapes pacing, chapter length, and reader expectation from page one.

entries.name: YA Fantasy: Voice, Agency, and the Coming-of-Age Contract
entries.description: Writing the young protagonist honestly rather than writing an adult who is sixteen.
entries.principle: YA is defined by protagonist age, voice, and thematic focus — identity formation, first autonomy, the discovery that adults are fallible — rather than by simplicity. The binding requirement is agency: the young protagonist's choices must drive the resolution, because a story where adults solve the problem betrays the form's central promise.
entries.example: Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea is the coming-of-age standard, Ged's error and its repair entirely his own; Pullman's His Dark Materials trusts young readers with theology and grief; Bardugo's Six of Crows runs ensemble YA with adult-grade plotting; the failure mode is the chosen teen whose mentors do the work.
entries.application: Keep adolescent priorities genuinely operative — loyalty, reputation, belonging, and first love should compete with saving the world and sometimes win. Solve the adult problem structurally: absent, fallible, hostile, or overwhelmed, but never merely stupid. And let the voice be young without being naive: interiority, immediacy, and a narrower time horizon rather than a smaller vocabulary.

entries.name: YA Fantasy: Darkness Calibration and the Hope Requirement
entries.description: Handling grief, violence, and despair for younger readers without lying to them.
entries.principle: YA fantasy handles death, war, abuse, and loss routinely; the calibration is not about subject but about camera placement and ending. The form's implicit contract is that the protagonist's agency matters and the future remains inhabitable — bleakness is permitted, futility is not, and readers finishing the book should believe that acting was better than not acting.
entries.example: Cooper's The Dark Is Rising and Alexander's Prydain kill characters and grieve properly; Pullman's ending is devastating and still leaves purpose intact; Adams's Watership Down is the middle-grade proof that death handled honestly is exactly why books endure; the failure modes are sanitizing until stakes vanish, and nihilism that leaves nothing to act on.
entries.application: Move the camera rather than the subject — aftermath, grief, and consequence get the page time that gore would take in adult work. Let costs be permanent, since reversible loss teaches nothing. And test the ending against the contract: if the protagonist's choices did not change the outcome, or if the outcome leaves no future worth having, the book has broken faith with its readership.

entries.name: Tie-In and Shared-World Craft
entries.description: Writing inside someone else's world, professionally.
