Note that Hellboy first appeared in *San Diego Comic-Con Comics* #2 in 1993, and that John Byrne scripted this first arc from Mignola's plot without co-creating the character. See Author 102.

entries.name: Fables
entries.author: Bill Willingham
entries.awards: Eisner Awards for Best New Series and Best Serialized Story, 2003
entries.description: Folklore characters exiled to a Manhattan enclave under an amnesty, and the best available demonstration of statecraft as a plot engine: the series…
entries.text: Folklore characters exiled to a Manhattan enclave under an amnesty, and the best available demonstration of statecraft as a plot engine: the series runs on treaty terms, succession disputes, security services and the farm where the non-human Fables are confined, so the stories generate from governance rather than from magic. Note the legal position — Willingham publicly declared the work public domain in 2023, DC immediately rejected this and asserts ownership, and the question is unlitigated, so the status is unresolved. Most of the fourteen Eisners belong to collaborators rather than to Willingham. See Author 104.

entries.name: Saga
entries.author: Brian K. Vaughan and Fiona Staples
entries.awards: Hugo Award, Best Graphic Story, 2013; multiple Eisner Awards
entries.description: Science fantasy that keeps its magic and its technology in the same frame without reconciling them, and the strongest recent argument that genre…
entries.text: Science fantasy that keeps its magic and its technology in the same frame without reconciling them, and the strongest recent argument that genre boundaries are a distribution convention. Its structural device is the retrospective narration of a child not yet born at the point the story begins, which guarantees survival for one character and therefore permits genuine jeopardy for everyone else — a clean solution to the serial fiction stakes problem. Staples's design work does most of the worldbuilding, with species and technology explained visually and never in dialogue. See Craft 26.

entries.name: Monstress
entries.author: Marjorie Liu and Sana Takeda
entries.awards: Hugo Award, Best Graphic Story, 2018; Eisner Award, Best Writer, 2018 — the first woman to win it
entries.description: Matriarchal art-deco Asian-influenced worldbuilding at a density unusual even in comics, with a protagonist sharing her body with an old god she cannot…
entries.text: Matriarchal art-deco Asian-influenced worldbuilding at a density unusual even in comics, with a protagonist sharing her body with an old god she cannot control. The craft interest for prose writers is the exposition strategy: Liu refuses almost all orientation, delivering political and racial history through overheard argument and an in-world lecture at each issue's end, which is the comics equivalent of Erikson's method. The war-crime and trauma material is handled with specificity rather than atmosphere. See Author 45 and Worldbuilding 5.

entries.name: Cardcaptor Sakura
entries.author: CLAMP
entries.awards: Seiun Award, Best Manga, 2001
entries.description: The magical-girl form at its most technically assured, and the clearest demonstration of CLAMP's page architecture — borderless bleeds, elongated…
entries.text: The magical-girl form at its most technically assured, and the clearest demonstration of CLAMP's page architecture — borderless bleeds, elongated figures crossing gutters, emotional state carried by layout rather than by dialogue. Its structural interest is the collection plot done properly: each card has a distinct personality and requires a different solution, so the episodic engine never repeats. Note the extensive editing of the English broadcast version, which removed the relationships that are central to the manga, and that CLAMP's shared multiverse means characters recur across unrelated series. See Author 106.

entries.name: Delicious in Dungeon
entries.author: Ryoko Kui
entries.description: A party descending a dungeon while cooking and eating the monsters, and a far more rigorous piece of worldbuilding than the premise suggests: Kui works…
entries.text: A party descending a dungeon while cooking and eating the monsters, and a far more rigorous piece of worldbuilding than the premise suggests: Kui works out monster ecology, nutrition, the economics of resurrection and the politics of the dungeon's surface administration, and the food is the delivery mechanism for all of it. It is the best modern example of the comic premise pursued with total seriousness until it becomes a coherent world. For writers working in games-adjacent fantasy it is the standing demonstration that examining the conventions is more productive than mocking them. See Worldbuilding 15 and Subgenre 29.

entries.name: Dungeons & Dragons
entries.author: Gary Gygax and Dave Arneson
entries.description: The single most consequential fantasy text after Tolkien, because it is how most working fantasy writers first encountered the genre as something you…
entries.text: The single most consequential fantasy text after Tolkien, because it is how most working fantasy writers first encountered the genre as something you make rather than something you read. It gave the field a shared vocabulary — classes, levels, alignment, hit points, the dungeon crawl, the adventuring party of mismatched specialists — and that vocabulary is now so naturalised that novels reproduce it unconsciously. Its magic system is Vance's, borrowed wholesale. Study it as a source of defaults to notice and choose about, rather than as a model. Co-created with Arneson, whose credit Gygax later contested and settled. See Author 107 and Work 23.

entries.name: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
entries.author: Nintendo; Shigeru Miyamoto, producer
entries.description: The game that established the modern three-dimensional adventure grammar, and for writers its interest is the structural use of time: an adult and a…
entries.text: The game that established the modern three-dimensional adventure grammar, and for writers its interest is the structural use of time: an adult and a child timeline that share a geography, so the same locations carry two states and the player's knowledge of one informs the other. That is a technique prose fantasy uses rarely and could use more. Its second lesson is environmental storytelling before the term existed — the world's history is legible in ruins, gravestones and songs rather than in dialogue. See Craft 32.

entries.name: Planescape: Torment
entries.author: Black Isle Studios; Chris Avellone, lead designer
entries.description: The most literary game ever made, with something near a million words, a combat system it actively discourages you from using, and a central question —…
entries.text: The most literary game ever made, with something near a million words, a combat system it actively discourages you from using, and a central question — what can change the nature of a man — that the entire design exists to interrogate. Its protagonist is an immortal amnesiac reassembling his own past crimes, so the exposition problem and the moral problem are the same problem. For writers it is the best demonstration that a fantasy setting built on ideas rather than on geography can sustain enormous length. Commercially unsuccessful and permanently influential. See Craft 25 and Psychology 11.

entries.name: Dark Souls
entries.author: FromSoftware; Hidetaka Miyazaki, dir.
entries.description: The work that made withheld information a design resource rather than a defect: the narrative is distributed into item descriptions, level topology and…
entries.text: The work that made withheld information a design resource rather than a defect: the narrative is distributed into item descriptions, level topology and NPC behaviour, deliberately incomplete, so reconstructing it is the experience. Its world geometry folds so that late areas loop back onto early ones, which makes spatial mastery itself the story of progression. For prose writers the transferable lesson is the confidence to leave the cosmology unstated and let the reader assemble it — the opposite of the appendix instinct, and considerably more effective when the fragments are consistent. See Author 108.

entries.name: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt
entries.author: CD Projekt Red
entries.awards: The Game Awards, Game of the Year, 2015
entries.description: The best-written quest design in the medium, and the reason is structural: the side quests refuse binary morality, so a monster contract routinely…
entries.text: The best-written quest design in the medium, and the reason is structural: the side quests refuse binary morality, so a monster contract routinely turns out to be a domestic tragedy in which the monster has the better case and no available outcome is clean. That is Sapkowski's actual method, faithfully translated. For writers it is a useful corrective to the assumption that moral complexity requires a grim tone — the game is frequently funny. It also made Sapkowski globally famous, and his separate dispute with the studio over his original flat-fee contract is part of the record. See Author 56 and Work 121.

entries.name: Baldur's Gate 3
entries.author: Larian Studios
entries.awards: The Game Awards, Game of the Year, 2023; BAFTA Best Game, 2024
entries.description: The most complete demonstration yet that a fantasy narrative can absorb genuine player authorship without collapsing: the branching accommodates…
entries.text: The most complete demonstration yet that a fantasy narrative can absorb genuine player authorship without collapsing: the branching accommodates outcomes most designers would have foreclosed, including killing characters the plot appears to require, and the writing holds. For prose writers the interest is in how much character work is doing the load-bearing — the companions have independent objectives and will leave — and in the reactivity discipline, where the world remembers small choices for dozens of hours. It also brought the Dungeons & Dragons rules to their largest audience in half a century. See Work 165.
